facts.statement: Barosaurus is a genus of dinosaur.
facts.quote: genus: Barosaurus

facts.statement: The only valid species in the genus is Barosaurus lentus.
facts.quote: species: lentus

facts.statement: Barosaurus affinis is considered a synonym of Barosaurus lentus.
facts.quote: synonyms: *Barosaurus affinis Marsh, 1899

facts.statement: Barosaurus was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1890.
facts.quote: It was described by American paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh in 1890.

facts.statement: Barosaurus lived in present-day North America during the Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: Barosaurus ( ) ("heavy lizard") is a genus of large sauropod dinosaur that lived in present-day North America during the Late Jurassic period.

facts.statement: Barosaurus lived during the Kimmeridgian stage, approximately 152 to 150 million years ago.
facts.quote: Barosaurus is known from the Kimmeridgian stage of the Late Jurassic period, which dates to around 152 to 150 million years ago.

facts.statement: Adult Barosaurus measured between 25 and 27 meters in length and weighed between 12 and 20 metric tons.
facts.quote: Barosaurus was an enormous animal, with some adults measuring about 25 - 27 m in length and weighing about 12–20 metric tons (13–22 short tons).

facts.statement: Compared to Diplodocus, Barosaurus had a relatively longer neck but a shorter tail.
facts.quote: In comparison to its close kin Diplodocus, Barosaurus has a relatively longer neck but shorter tail.

facts.statement: Barosaurus possessed 16 cervical vertebrae, which were extremely elongated.
facts.quote: Barosaurus has 16 cervical vertebrae, more than Diplodocus and Apatosaurus, which are extremely elongated.

facts.statement: Barosaurus had a compact back consisting of only nine dorsal vertebrae.
facts.quote: The back was more compact, with only nine dorsal vertebrae.

facts.statement: Specimens of Barosaurus have been found in the Morrison Formation in Utah and Montana, with potential fossils reported from Colorado, Wyoming, and Oklahoma.
facts.quote: Several other specimens have been collected outcrops of the Morrison Formation in Utah and Montana, though fossils potentially from the genus have been reported from Colorado, Wyoming, and Oklahoma as well.

facts.statement: The initial type specimen consisted of six tail vertebrae, which Marsh named Barosaurus lentus.
facts.quote: Only six tail vertebrae were recovered at that time, forming the type specimen (YPM 429) of a new species, which Marsh named Barosaurus lentus.

facts.statement: Marsh first classified Barosaurus as a diplodocid in 1898, after previously placing it in Atlantosauridae in 1896.
facts.quote: In 1896 Marsh had placed Barosaurus in the Atlantosauridae; in 1898 it was classified by him as a diplodocid for the first time.

facts.statement: Four neck vertebrae, each 1 meter long, were collected in 1912 and later identified as belonging to Barosaurus by William Jacob Holland.
facts.quote: Four neck vertebrae, each 1 meter (3 feet) long, were collected in 1912 near a specimen of Diplodocus, but a few years later, William Jacob Holland realized they belonged to a different species.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Barosaurus was fully described by Richard Swann Lull in 1919.
facts.quote: The type specimen of Barosaurus had finally been prepared at Yale in the winter of 1917 and was fully described by Richard Swann Lull in 1919.

facts.statement: A cast of a Barosaurus specimen was controversially mounted in the American Museum of Natural History lobby rearing up to defend its young from an Allosaurus.
facts.quote: A cast of this specimen (AMNH 6341) was controversially mounted in the lobby of the American Museum, rearing up to defend its young (AMNH 7530, now classified as Kaatedocus siberi) from an attacking Allosaurus fragilis.

facts.statement: Barosaurus is among the largest diplodocid sauropods.
facts.quote: This makes it among the largest diplodocid sauropods.

facts.statement: It is debated how Barosaurus was depicted in popular media, with Darren Naish noting that late 20th-century books often incorrectly showed it as a short-tailed sauropod with a U-shaped neck.
facts.quote: Darren Naish has noted a common error in books of the late 20th century to depict Barosaurus as a kind of brachiosaur-like short tailed sauropod with raphes on its neck and body, and often curving the upper half of its neck downwards into a U-shape, citing it as an example of a Palaeoart meme.

facts.statement: A Barosaurus specimen was excavated by Earl Douglass at the Carnegie Quarry in the early 20th century and later traded to the Royal Ontario Museum in 1962.
facts.quote: Another specimen excavated by Earl Douglass at Carnegie Quarry in the early 20th century was acquired by the Royal Ontario Museum (ROM) in Toronto in a 1962 trade with the Carnegie Museum.

facts.statement: Paleontologist David Evans discovered a forgotten Barosaurus skeleton in the Royal Ontario Museum collection in 2007.
facts.quote: In 2007, the newly appointed curator of the ROM, paleontologist David Evans, was flying to the U.S. Badlands when he discovered a literature reference to a Barosaurus skeleton in the ROM collection.

facts.statement: Adult Barosaurus measured about 25 to 27 meters in length and weighed between 12 and 20 metric tons.
facts.quote: Barosaurus was an enormous animal, with some adults measuring about 25 - 27 m in length and weighing about 12–20 metric tons (13–22 short tons).

facts.statement: Barosaurus had a longer neck and shorter tail than Diplodocus but was about the same overall length.
facts.quote: Barosaurus was differently proportioned than its close relative Diplodocus, with a longer neck and shorter tail, but was about the same length overall.

facts.statement: No Barosaurus skull has ever been discovered.
facts.quote: Scientists have yet to discover a Barosaurus skull.

facts.statement: In 2017, researchers assigned an incomplete juvenile diplodocid skeleton found at Dinosaur National Monument to Barosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2017, American researcher Keegan M. Melstrom and colleagues assigned an incomplete juvenile diplodocid skeleton (DINO 2921) that had been found at Dinosaur National Monument to Barosaurus.

facts.statement: Barosaurus had only 9 dorsal vertebrae, whereas Diplodocus and Apatosaurus had 10.
facts.quote: Diplodocus and Apatosaurus both had 15 cervical (neck) and 10 dorsal (trunk) vertebrae, while Barosaurus had only 9 dorsals.

facts.statement: A dorsal vertebra may have been converted into a cervical one, resulting in a total of 16 neck vertebrae in Barosaurus.
facts.quote: A dorsal may have been converted into a cervical vertebra, for a total of 16 vertebrae in the neck.

facts.statement: Some Barosaurus neck vertebrae were up to 50% longer than those of Diplodocus.
facts.quote: Barosaurus cervicals were similar to those of Diplodocus, but some were up to 50% longer.

facts.statement: The Barosaurus tail likely ended in a long whiplash, similar to other diplodocids which could have up to 80 tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: The tail probably ended in a long whiplash, much like Apatosaurus, Diplodocus and other diplodocids, some of which had up to 80 tail vertebrae.

facts.statement: Paleontologists suspected that Barosaurus africanus was distinct from the North American genus, a view confirmed by a 2006 redescription.
facts.quote: Many paleontologists suspected "Barosaurus" africanus was also distinct from the North American genus, which was confirmed when the material was redescribed in 2006.

facts.statement: A 1987 identification of a Barosaurus species from the Kadsi Formation in Zimbabwe is considered doubtful due to poor preservation and inadequate diagnosis.
facts.quote: A species of Barosaurus was also allegedly identified from the Kadsi Formation in Zimbabwe in 1987. However, this material is poorly preserved and fragmentary and was not adequately diagnosed as such, and so its referral to Barosaurus is doubtful.

facts.statement: Barosaurus had limb bones that were virtually indistinguishable from those of Diplodocus.
facts.quote: The limb bones of Barosaurus were virtually indistinguishable from those of Diplodocus.

facts.statement: Barosaurus was a quadruped with columnar limbs adapted to support its enormous bulk.
facts.quote: Both were quadrupedal, with columnar limbs adapted to support the enormous bulk of the animals.

facts.statement: Although Barosaurus feet have never been discovered, it would have been digitigrade with five small toes on each of its four feet.
facts.quote: Barosaurus feet have never been discovered, but like other sauropods, it would have been digitigrade, with all four feet each bearing five small toes.

facts.statement: Barosaurus had a large claw on the inside digit of its forefoot and smaller claws on the inside three digits of its hindfoot.
facts.quote: A large claw adorned the inside digit on the manus (forefoot) while smaller claws tipped the inside three digits of the pes (hindfoot).

facts.statement: Barosaurus is classified as a member of the sauropod family Diplodocidae and is sometimes placed in the subfamily Diplodocinae with Diplodocus.
facts.quote: Barosaurus is a member of the sauropod family Diplodocidae, and sometimes placed with Diplodocus in the subfamily Diplodocinae.

facts.statement: Many paleontologists consider the genus Seismosaurus to be a junior synonym of Diplodocus, potentially representing a fourth species.
facts.quote: Another diplodocid genus, Seismosaurus, is considered by many paleontologists to be a junior synonym of Diplodocus as a possible fourth species.

facts.statement: Tornieria (formerly Barosaurus africanus) and Australodocus from the Tendaguru Beds of Tanzania have been classified as diplodocines.
facts.quote: Tornieria (formerly "Barosaurus" africanus) and Australodocus from the famous Tendaguru Beds of Tanzania in eastern Africa have also been classified as diplodocines.

facts.statement: Diplodocid fossils, including those of Barosaurus, are found in North America, Europe, and Africa.
facts.quote: Diplodocid fossils are found in North America, Europe, and Africa.

facts.statement: A 2016 preprint by Mike Taylor and Mathew Wedel argued that Barosaurus cervical vertebrae allowed significant lateral neck flexibility but restricted vertical flexibility.
facts.quote: In a 2016 preprint, Mike Taylor and Mathew Wedel argued that the structure of the cervical vertebrae of Barosaurus allowed for a significant degree of lateral flexibility in the neck, but restricted vertical flexibility.

facts.statement: The neck structure suggests Barosaurus had a different feeding style compared to other diplodocids.
facts.quote: This suggests a different feeding style for this genus when compared to other diplodocids.

facts.statement: The restriction in vertical neck flexibility suggests Barosaurus did not primarily feed on vegetation high off the ground.
facts.quote: The restriction in vertical flexibility suggests that Barosaurus did not primarily feed on vegetation that was high off the ground.

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that a nuchal ligament may have held Barosaurus' neck in a horizontal position.
facts.quote: A nuchal ligament may have held the neck in this position.

facts.statement: An alternative hypothesis suggests Barosaurus possessed an avian-like elastic ligament similar to that seen in Struthio camelus.
facts.quote: Another hypothesized neck-supporting ligament is an avian-like elastic ligament, such as that seen in Struthio camelus.

facts.statement: A 2009 study argued that sauropods likely held their necks at maximum vertical extension in an alert posture, barring unknown unique soft tissue characteristics.
facts.quote: A 2009 study found that all tetrapods appear to hold the base of their necks at the maximum possible vertical extension when in a normal, alert posture, and argued that the same would hold true for sauropods barring any unknown, unique characteristics that set the soft tissue anatomy of their necks apart from other animals.

facts.statement: This idea of an elevated neck pose might be contradicted by evidence that the inner ear of diplodocoids aligns with a horizontal neck pose.
facts.quote: However, this idea might be contradicted due to the inner ear of diplodocoids actually being in alignment for a horizontal neck pose.

facts.statement: A 1992 study suggested that Barosaurus would have needed a heart weighing 1.6 tons to pump blood up its very long neck.
facts.quote: A 1992 Columbia University study of diplodocid neck structure indicated that the longest necks would have required a 1.6-ton heart

facts.statement: Some scientists hypothesize that Barosaurus possessed auxiliary hearts in its neck to assist blood circulation.
facts.quote: The study proposed that animals like these would have had rudimentary auxiliary "hearts" in their necks

facts.statement: Researchers debate whether Barosaurus held its neck horizontally to avoid the challenge of pumping blood to its brain.
facts.quote: Some argue that the near-horizontal posture of the head and neck would have eliminated the problem of supplying blood to the brain

facts.statement: Barosaurus lived approximately 150 million years ago during the late Kimmeridgian to early Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: Barosaurus fossils are found in late Kimmeridgian to early Tithonian sediments, around 150 million years old

facts.statement: Barosaurus shared its environment with other giant sauropods including Camarasaurus, Diplodocus, Apatosaurus, and Brachiosaurus.
facts.quote: The Morrison Formation records an environment and time dominated by gigantic sauropod dinosaurs such as Camarasaurus, Diplodocus, Apatosaurus and Brachiosaurus

facts.statement: Herbivorous ornithischians such as Camptosaurus, Dryosaurus, Stegosaurus, and Othnielosaurus lived alongside Barosaurus.

facts.statement: Barosaurus faced predators including theropods like Saurophaganax, Allosaurus, Torvosaurus, Ceratosaurus, Marshosaurus, Stokesosaurus, and Ornitholestes.

facts.statement: Allosaurus made up 70 to 75% of theropod fossils found in the Morrison Formation and occupied the top trophic level.

facts.statement: High atmospheric carbon dioxide levels during the Late Jurassic created a greenhouse effect with global high temperatures.

facts.statement: The climate in the Barosaurus habitat was semi-arid with seasonal rainfall due to high evaporation and rain shadows from western mountains.
